newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Analysts wary on GIB despite Sarma talks.
newsitem.headline: Analysts wary on GIB despite Sarma talks.

text.p: News that Belgian retail group GIB is in talks with Dutch Hema to sell its speciality retail chain Sarma was welcomed by analysts on Tuesday, but several said it would not change their cautious view on the GIB stock.

"If Sarma is out of the group, the absence of the chain means an absence of losses (from Sarma). But I continue to be very cautious on GIB," said KB-Securities analyst Michel Ernst, adding he viewed the stock as "very speculative".
He cited competition faced by GIB's GB supermarkets as well as the performance of the home-improvement sector (DIY) and GIB unit Quick Restaurants as reasons for his concern.

GIB - which had been saying for months it was seeking a partner for Sarma - is negotiating with Dutch department store chain Hema, a unit of NV Koninklijke Bijenkorf Beheer (KBB), for Hema to take over Sarma stores.

GIB has been re-positioning the chain by remodelling some stores, closing down others and developing its own brand, but it said on Monday Sarma "no longer responded to the requirements of a textile sector which was becoming increasingly global".
By the end of GIB's first half 1996/1997 financial year Sarma had 28 stores. GIB's financial year runs to March 31.

Analysts said Sarma's small size made it hard for the chain to compete with European competitors established in Belgium and it had also been hurt by weak demand in Belgium, particularly for new clothes.
GIB said the impact of the Sarma sale on its consolidated accounts would be around 200 million Belgian francs ($6 million) "essentially due to the exceptional amortization of assets".
"This is not so heavy compared to the recurrent losses of Sarma," said Stephane Roffler at Mignon Hanart Declerck.

Thierry Masset, analyst at BBL/Vermeulen-Raemdonck, said the stock remained a 'hold' in anticipation of more information from the group and the publication of 1996/1997 earnings. "We could become more positive later," he added.
He said the 200 million franc figure was "not a huge amount in absolute terms for GIB" but large for a unit Sarma's size.

The divestment would be the latest in a series for GIB which has included the sale of its stake in Sodal, the operator in Belgium of French hi-fi, photo and mulit-media chain FNAC, and of its 25 percent interest in U.K. based DIY chain Homebase.

In 1995 GIB sold its 65 percent stake in loss-making U.S. home improvement (DIY) chain Handy Andy, for which it booked a 5.5 billion franc exceptional charge that weighed on 1995/1996 full year earnings.
GIB made a group loss of 4.39 billion francs in 1995/1996 after a group net profit of 2.17 billion in 1994/1995.
Turnover in 1995/1996 was 228 billion francs and GIB made a first half 1996/1997 group net profit of 2.5 billion francs.
GIB has also been saying for some time it is looking for a partner for Inno, another of the group's speciality retailers, to boost the department store chain's buying power.
As a sector, speciality retailing contributed eight percent to total sales in 1995/1996, but only 0.2 percent to operating profit.

GIB's general manager of speciality retailing, Raymond Vaxelaire, said in the group's 1995/1996 annual report the division should "focus all our efforts on sectors with strong prospects and eliminate those sectors without a specific future".

By contrast GIB's restaurants, which also accounted for eight percent of turnover, contributed a solid 38.9 percent of profits, for supermarkets the figures were 63 percent and 24.5 percent respectively. The home-improvements division made up 21 percent of sales and 36.4 percent of operating profit.
GIB shares extended their recent rally to close 55 francs or 3.3 percent higher at 1,565 francs on the Brussels bourse on Tuesday, their highest close since March last year.
